title: Blocking a needlepoint canvas
subtitle: Stretching and squaring the finished canvas before mounting
excerpt: Needlepoint canvas often distorts during work, particularly under diagonal tent stitches. Blocking is the process of wetting and pinning the canvas square on a board while it dries. The canvas stays in its corrected shape once dry.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), finishing chapter. Weldon's Practical Needlework, canvaswork series.

glossaryTerms.definition: Wetting a finished needlepoint piece and pinning it square to a board while it dries. The wet canvas threads relax and hold their corrected position as they dry.

heroPrompt: A needlepoint canvas pinned to a foam blocking board with T-pins, slightly damp, squared to a right-angle template, natural light.

content.text: Most needlepoint canvases distort during work. Tent stitch, in particular, pulls the canvas diagonally. The corners of a finished tent-stitch piece often point rather than sitting square.
corrects this. The process takes a few minutes to set up, then the canvas dries overnight.

items.label: Blocking board
items.value: A piece of softboard, thick foam, or a folded-towel stack large enough for the canvas. Must take pins without splitting

items.label: Pins
items.value: Stainless-steel T-pins or rustproof sewing pins, one every 2 cm around the perimeter

items.label: Set square or right-angle tool
items.value: To check the corners are truly square as you pin

items.label: Clean water
items.value: A bowl or plant mister of clean water at room temperature. Do not use hot water

items.label: Ruler
items.value: To verify the canvas dimensions as you stretch

content.text: How to block a needlepoint canvas
Mist the canvas lightly with water on both sides, or dampen it with a wet cloth. The canvas should be evenly damp but not soaking. Wool threads relax once wet and will take a new shape as they dry.
Lay the canvas right-side-down on the blocking board. Pin one corner with two T-pins, making sure the canvas threads run square to the board edges.
Pull the opposite corner square and pin it. Use a set square to check both corners are right angles before adding more pins.

Pin the two remaining corners, then fill in the pins every 2 cm around the perimeter, pulling the canvas straight as you go. The canvas should feel taut but should not be stretched so hard the threads pucker.
Leave the canvas pinned to the board overnight. Check it is fully dry before removing the pins. A damp canvas will distort again as soon as the pins come out.

Very heavily distorted canvases, particularly those worked in continental tent stitch without a frame, may need two blocking sessions. Unpin, re-dampen, and re-pin a second time. The canvas usually straightens fully after two sessions.

Basketweave tent stitch distorts the canvas far less than continental because its back threads run in alternating directions. Bargello distorts it differently, pulling upward rather than diagonally. Any tent-stitch piece worked without a frame will need blocking. Pieces mounted on a scroll frame throughout often need only a light block or none at all.
